edits.find: Fever with seizure under 6 months, or with a full fontanelle or prolonged drowsiness, is a lumbar puncture — and an open fontanelle needs no CT. · The febrile-seizure diagnosis has an age gate on both ends, 6 months and 5 years, and it is the fastest disqualifier on the topic — check it before anything else. · An open fontanelle is a pop-off valve, which is why infants tolerate rising intracranial pressure that would herniate an older child, and why the CT-before-tap rule generally does not apply to them. · The same finding can be both the indication and the apparent contraindication; when that happens, ask what the rule is protecting against, and whether that risk exists in this patient. · Infants do not have neck signs — read the fontanelle, the tone, the suck and the cry instead, because a supple neck excludes nothing under about 18 months ⚠︎. · A postictal period beyond 10 minutes is not a long febrile seizure, it is altered mental status, and it earns a tap on its own. · With petechiae and hypotension the order inverts: antibiotics first, tap after, because a sterilised Gram stain is an acceptable price.

edits.find:
A child with a VP shunt presents with vomiting, irritability, lethargy, and hypertension — four signs of increased intracranial pressure. The diagnostic reflex for raised ICP is neuroimaging, and the specific concern is shunt malfunction causing recurrent obstructive hydrocephalus. CT of the head is the first step — it shows whether the ventricles have re-dilated.

The miss: choosing LP. LP is contraindicated in obstructive hydrocephalus — the pressure gradient between the ventricles and the lumbar subarachnoid space can cause transtentorial herniation. In a shunt patient, CSF is obtained by tapping the shunt reservoir, never by lumbar puncture.

LP is contraindicated in obstructive hydrocephalus; the pressure gradient between the ventricles and the lumbar subarachnoid space can cause transtentorial herniation.
